title: Two men to stand trial over ‘transnational criminal organisation’ behind sports piracy site
content:
Two men will stand trial in Egypt for running a “transnational criminal organisation” behind illegal sports piracy site Streameast, according to law enforcement officials in the North African country.

The Athletic broke the news in September that the men were arrested on the outskirts of Cairo following a year-long investigation into a network of over 120 domains with an annual audience of 1.6 billion, the largest to have been taken down by authorities. The operation involved 22 officers in two locations.

The site which cloned characteristics from other — and still active — Streameast sites provided free access to a wide range of global sports fixtures including Premier League, Champions League, NFL, NBA and MLB.

The Egyptian nationals — arrested on suspicion of copyright infringement — were discovered to have generated £7.6million in advertising revenue from the site with approximately £450,000 in multiple crypto wallets. Laptops used to operate the site, smartphones, credit cards — containing approximately £95,000 — and cash were seized in addition to documents related to shell companies and real estate.

Police released a photograph of them (with heads obscured) standing in front of the items seized in the raid. The Athletic has learned their professions, but due to ongoing legal proceedings, we are not yet permitted to reveal the information.

The suspects were detained following the arrests on August 25, 2025 whilst investigations continued. On Monday, Egypt’s Attorney General’s office released a statement “ordering the referral of two defendants to criminal trial” for “establishing and managing a transnational criminal organisation specialising in pirating sports broadcasts and violating intellectual property rights”.

In addition to a copycat version of Streameast, the statement also revealed that the pair were also running a version of CrackStreams, which also provides pirated live sports feeds.

The case was initially referred to Egypt’s intellectual property investigators by the Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment (ACE), a U.S. headed organisation which represents 50 global media and entertainment companies.

The Athletic spoke to one of ACE’s investigators Dani Bacsa in a special audio documentary — The Underground World of Illegal Streaming — who explained that the “majority of the traffic going to that service came from the U.S., from Canada or the UK” and its resistance to takedown notices made it “a high priority target”. On average 136 million people watched sports action on the site each month.

The investigation monitored trends, traffic and used legal discovery tools (which can oblige legitimate service providers that may unknowingly be linked to a criminal operation to provide information) to discover an IP address in Egypt. From there, “digital breadcrumbs” were followed which showed “an offshore shell company that funnelled the funds to two locations: one in the APAC (Asian-Pacific) region and one in Dubai”.

Egyptian authorities said that “the defendants managed the piracy network through hundreds of electronic domains and an integrated technical infrastructure to broadcast encrypted sports content without a license, generating significant financial returns from international advertising”.

Money laundering charges are included within the indictment following cyber crime investigations due to the defendants concealing “proceeds of their criminal activity by purchasing real estate, establishing a front company abroad and using cryptocurrencies and cross-border financial platforms,” said the Attorney General’s statement.

It also read: “The Public Prosecution affirms its continued decisive response to cybercrimes, tracking down digital piracy networks and tracing their illegal proceeds, within the framework of international judicial cooperation and in a manner that ensures the protection of intellectual property rights and the preservation of the national economy.”

It is estimated that piracy costs the sports industry £20billion a year, but due to cost and the convenience of illegal streaming sites it is increasingly popular. The Athletic surveyed over 5,000 people and 47 per cent of respondents — subscribers from around the world, who took part anonymously — said they watch football via illegal streams.

“I’m under no illusion that I’ve obliterated the Streameast brand off the face of the earth,” Larissa Knapp — who spearheads the Motion Picture Association’s long-term anti-piracy operations — told The Athletic following the initial takedown. “When we take one down, five more will come up or more, because folks have that brand recognition.”
